{{Short description|Geographic sampling}}
An '''area sampling frame''' is an alternative to the most traditional type of [[sampling frame]]s.

A sampling frame is often defined as a list of elements of the population we want to explore through a [[sample survey]]. A slightly more general concept considers that a sampling frame is a tool that allows the identification and access to the elements of the population, even if an explicit list does not exist.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Handbook on Master Sampling Frames for Agricultural Statistics |url=https://docplayer.net/18720914-Handbook-on-master-sampling-frames-for-agricultural-statistics.html |access-date=2023-12-11 |website=docplayer.net}}</ref> Traditional sampling frames are sometimes referred to as ''list frames''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Turner |first=Anthony G. |date=5 December 2003 |title=Sampling frames and master samples |url=https://mdgs.un.org/unsd/demographic/meetings/egm/Sampling_1203/docs/no_3.pdf |access-date=January 6, 2024 |website=Millenium development goals indicators}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Carfagna |first=Elisabetta |date=2015 |title=Combining list frames with different kinds of area frame |url=https://2015.isiproceedings.org/Files/STS006-P4-S.pdf |access-date=January 6, 2024 |website=International Statistical Institute, 60th ISI World Statistics Congress Proceedings}}</ref>

In many cases, suitable lists are not available. This can happen for several reasons, for example:

* Existing lists, such as [[Census|population censuses]], are too old and do not correspond anymore to the current reality.
* We are targeting a population whose list is not feasible, for example a wild animal species.
* The population is a continuous feature in a given geographic area and the definition of its elements is not straightforward. This often happens for sample surveys designed to produce [[environmental statistics]].

Area sampling frames are generally defined by two elements:

* The boundaries of a target region in a given [[Map projection|cartographic projection]].
* The type of geographic units to be sampled. We can mention three main types of units:
** Points. In principle, points are dimensionless, but, for practical reasons, we can attribute them a certain size, such as 1 m × 1 m. The suitable size is linked to the accuracy of the tool used for the location of the point. Possible tools are [[Global Positioning System|GPS]] devices, [[orthophoto]]s or [[Satellite imagery|satellite images]]. Point sampling can be based on a two-stage scheme, sampling clusters in the first stage and sampling points in the second stage. Another option is a two-phase scheme of unclustered points: a large first-phase sample is selected. A stratification is conducted only for the first-phase sample and a stratified sample is chosen in the second phase.
** [[Transect]]s. A transect is a piece of straight line of a given length. Transect sampling is useful to estimate the total length of linear landscape elements
** Areal units defined by polygons. In the jargon of agricultural surveys, areal units are generally called "segments",<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Boryan |first1=Claire |last2=Yang |first2=Zhengwei |last3=Di |first3=Liping |last4=Hunt |first4=Kevin |date=November 2014 |title=A New Automatic Stratification Method for U.S. Agricultural Area Sampling Frame Construction Based on the Cropland Data Layer |journal=IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Applied Earth Observations and Remote Sensing |volume=7 |issue=11 |pages=4317–4327 |doi=10.1109/JSTARS.2014.2322584 |bibcode=2014IJSTA...7.4317B |s2cid=11727236 |issn=1939-1404}}</ref> even if a segment in geometry rather corresponds to the concept of transect used in area sampling frames. Segments can be delineated by photo-interpretation or generated automatically, usually on the basis of a regular grid.<ref name=":0" /> The optimal size of segments depends on the [[spatial auto-correlation]] of the monitored processes and the [[Cost function (economics)|cost function]] that links the price of data collection with the size of the sample unit<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Gallego |first=Francisco Javier |date=2012-03-20 |title=The efficiency of sampling very high resolution images for area estimation in the European Union |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01431161.2011.602993 |journal=International Journal of Remote Sensing |language=en |volume=33 |issue=6 |pages=1868–1880 |doi=10.1080/01431161.2011.602993 |bibcode=2012IJRS...33.1868G |s2cid=128680455 |issn=0143-1161|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Fields of application ==
The oldest field of application area sampling frames has been probably [[Forest inventory|forest inventories]], one of the fields with the most obvious geographic component in which the traditional list frame approach cannot be applied. For the same reason, area frames appear as a natural tool for many environmental topics, such as [[soil survey]]s and other topics that require [[spatial statistics]] tools.

Different area frame approaches have been widely discussed and compared for agricultural statistics. In the 1930s, the [[National Agricultural Statistics Service]] of the [[United States Department of Agriculture|US Department of Agriculture]] introduced area sampling frames for the estimation of crop area and yield on the basis of a sample of areal units (segments<ref name=":1" />). The French Teruti survey<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chakir |first1=Raja |last2=Laurent |first2=Thibault |last3=Ruiz-Gazen |first3=Anne |last4=Thomas-Agnan |first4=Christine |last5=Vignes |first5=Céline |date=November 2016 |title=Spatial scale in land use models: Application to the Teruti-Lucas survey |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S2211675316300331 |journal=Spatial Statistics |language=en |volume=18 |pages=246–262 |doi=10.1016/j.spasta.2016.06.009|bibcode=2016SpaSt..18..246C |url-access=subscription }}</ref> chose in the 1960s an approach based on a [[Systematic sampling|systematic sample]] of clusters of points. The Italian AGRIT survey has explored different approaches, comparing segment and point methods.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Agricultural survey methods: based on papers presented at the 1998, 2001, 2004 and 2007 International Conferences on Agricultural Statistics |date=2010 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-0-470-74371-3 |editor-last=Benedetti |editor-first=Roberto |location=Chichester}}</ref> The [[Joint Research Centre]] of the EC has conducted a large number of studies on area sampling frame methodology and area frame surveys for agricultural, forestry, environmental and human settlement studies.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Gallego Pinilla |first=Francisco |title=Area Sampling frames for Agricultural and Environmental Statistics: Short guidelines for developing countries |publisher=Publications Office of the European Union |year=2015 |isbn=978-92-79-54000-4 |location=Luxembourg |pages=3–25 |language=English}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tenerelli |first1=Patrizia |last2=Gallego |first2=Javier F. |last3=Ehrlich |first3=Daniele |date=September 2015 |title=Population density modelling in support of disaster risk assessment |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S2212420915300431 |journal=International Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction |language=en |volume=13 |pages=334–341 |doi=10.1016/j.ijdrr.2015.07.015|bibcode=2015IJDRR..13..334T |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

The soaring number of applications of [[Satellite imagery|satellite images]] has boosted the interest on area sampling frames, not only because of the use of [[remote sensing for statistics]] and because the integration of satellite images has improved the quality of sampling frames and related estimators,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Carfagna |first1=Elisabetta |last2=Gallego |first2=F. Javier |date=2006-12-14 |title=Using Remote Sensing for Agricultural Statistics |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1751-5823.2005.tb00155.x |journal=International Statistical Review |language=en |volume=73 |issue=3 |pages=389–404 |doi=10.1111/j.1751-5823.2005.tb00155.x|s2cid=15112469 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> but also because satellite images may need to be sampled.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Achard |first1=Frédéric |last2=Eva |first2=Hugh D. |last3=Stibig |first3=Hans-Jürgen |last4=Mayaux |first4=Philippe |last5=Gallego |first5=Javier |last6=Richards |first6=Timothy |last7=Malingreau |first7=Jean-Paul |date=2002-08-09 |title=Determination of Deforestation Rates of the World's Humid Tropical Forests |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1070656 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=297 |issue=5583 |pages=999–1002 |doi=10.1126/science.1070656 |pmid=12169731 |bibcode=2002Sci...297..999A |s2cid=46315941 |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Validation of thematic maps produced by satellite image analysis has become one of the main application fields of area sampling frames.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Olofsson |first1=Pontus |last2=Foody |first2=Giles M. |last3=Herold |first3=Martin |last4=Stehman |first4=Stephen V. |last5=Woodcock |first5=Curtis E. |last6=Wulder |first6=Michael A. |date=2014-05-25 |title=Good practices for estimating area and assessing accuracy of land change |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0034425714000704 |journal=Remote Sensing of Environment |volume=148 |pages=42–57 |doi=10.1016/j.rse.2014.02.015 |bibcode=2014RSEnv.148...42O |issn=0034-4257}}</ref>
